analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in January 2015 and never received a hearing or a vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the federal estate tax (the tax paid on very large inheritances), along with the gift tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, effective immediately upon enactment [S3][S2]. The estate tax applies only to estates above a large exemption — roughly $5.4 million per person in 2015 under law then in effect — and fewer than two of every 1,000 estates owed any estate tax [widely reported]. The bill would therefore cut taxes exclusively for the heirs of the wealthiest families, while removing an estimated tens of billions of dollars a year in federal revenue that would otherwise come from those estates [widely reported]. It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: The heirs of the largest estates — families with wealth well into the millions — would pay nothing on inherited wealth. Very wealthy households could also make unlimited tax-free gifts during life once the gift tax was repealed [S3]. Farmers and small-business owners with large estates would gain some, but since the tax already shields most farm and business estates through exemptions and special valuation rules, the largest gains would go to the biggest fortunes [widely reported].

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax entirely [S3].
The CRS summary describes the bill as repealing the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes [S2].
Repeal would apply to deaths and gifts occurring after enactment, so affected families would owe nothing on transfers from that point forward [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The general public pays, in two ways: the federal treasury loses the revenue the estate tax raises (roughly $20 billion or more per year at the time), which must be made up through other taxes, deeper deficits, or spending cuts [widely reported]; and a progressive tax that falls only on very large inheritances disappears, shifting the overall tax burden toward work and wages.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate tax would cost the federal government a substantial amount of revenue — tens of billions of dollars annually — increasing deficits or requiring other taxes or spending cuts to offset it [widely reported].

The estate tax applies only to estates above a multi-million-dollar exemption; repealing it is a tax cut concentrated on the top fraction of one percent of estates, providing no benefit to the overwhelming majority of taxpayers [widely reported].

Even supporters of estate tax relief generally pursued expansion of exemptions or spousal portability rather than full repeal, acknowledging repeal's fiscal cost; this bill offered no revenue replacement [widely reported].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a tax cut for a very small, very wealthy group — heirs to estates above roughly $5.4 million per person in 2015. The cost is losing one of the most progressive taxes in the federal code, with the revenue burden shifting to everyone else through deficits or other taxes. Some farm families do face planning burdens under the current tax, but the tax already shelters most farm estates, so the bill's title overstates the case it makes. On balance the costs fall far more broadly than the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Hudson (R-NC) introduced the bill on January 7, 2015, the opening day of the 114th Congress [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
No further action appears in the record for the remainder of the 114th Congress, which ended January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the federal estate tax remained in place — ordinary taxpayers are spared the revenue loss and any offsetting tax increase. A repeal with no cosponsors posed little risk from the start.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The general public, which keeps the estate tax

for.name: Rep. Richard Hudson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; it was a Republican-sponsored bill with zero cosponsors of any party, suggesting little interest even among the majority [S4].

industries.industry: Heirs and families of the wealthiest estates
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated the tax owed on very large inheritances, a benefit limited to a tiny fraction of estates. The cost — lost revenue — is spread across everyone else, so the industry's gain runs against the public's.

Full repeal would have sharply reduced demand for trust and estate-planning services built around the current tax. The public effect is neutral to mildly positive; the loss is concentrated in this profession.

The bill's title targets farm and business estates, which do face planning costs under the tax. But the tax already shelters most farm estates through exemptions and special-use valuation, so the practical gain for most farms is modest while the largest benefits go to the biggest fortunes.
